items.stem: Which metal reacts with cold water to form an alkaline solution and hydrogen?
items.answer: calcium
items.markingKey: K, Na and Ca react with cold water: Ca + 2H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ + H₂.

items.stem: Explain why magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water but vigorously with steam.
items.answer: Steam particles have more energy (higher temperature), so more collisions have enough energy to react; also steam gives magnesium oxide on a hot surface.

items.stem: Explain why potassium and dilute hydrochloric acid are never reacted in a school laboratory.
items.answer: Potassium is so reactive that the reaction would be explosive.

items.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: formulae [1]; balancing [1]

items.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of magnesium with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂: formulae [1]; balancing [1]; state symbols [1]

items.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of zinc with dilute hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
items.markingKey: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂: formulae [1]; balancing [1]; state symbols [1]

items.stem: Samuel investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; Q: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — reacts steadily with fizzing; R: cold water — reacts vigorously, fizzing and moving around on the surface; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; S: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing. (a) Which metal(s) are below hydrogen in the reactivity series? Explain. (b) Name the gas produced when metals react with dilute acids and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) P: they do not react with dilute acid. (b) Hydrogen — lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: Mateo investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; Q: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — reacts steadily with fizzing; R: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles; S: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test. (a) P is magnesium. Write the equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid. (b) Name the gas produced when metals react with dilute acids and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ (b) Hydrogen — lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: Which products form when magnesium reacts with steam?
items.answer: magnesium oxide and hydrogen
items.markingKey: Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂.

items.stem: Which list is in order of decreasing reactivity?
items.answer: sodium, magnesium, zinc, copper
items.markingKey: Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > (C) > Zn > Fe > (H) > Cu > Ag > Au.

items.stem: Describe how you could use dilute hydrochloric acid to put zinc, iron and magnesium into a reactivity order.
items.answer: Add equal-sized pieces to equal volumes of the same acid at the same temperature; compare the rate of bubbling (or gas volume in a set time); faster = more reactive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fair test; 1 mark rate observation [2]

items.stem: Explain why the reaction of calcium with water makes the water turn cloudy.
items.answer: Calcium hydroxide is formed, which is only slightly soluble, so some appears as a white solid.

items.stem: A student says, "Aluminium must be less reactive than iron because aluminium saucepans do not corrode." Explain why the student is wrong.
items.answer: Aluminium is more reactive than iron, but it is protected by a thin, unreactive oxide layer.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the reaction of calcium with water makes the water turn cloudy. (b) Describe how you could use dilute hydrochloric acid to put zinc, iron and magnesium into a reactivity order.
items.answer: (a) Calcium hydroxide is formed, which is only slightly soluble, so some appears as a white solid. (b) Add equal-sized pieces to equal volumes of the same acid at the same temperature; compare the rate of bubbling (or gas volume in a set time); faster = more reactive.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark fair test; 1 mark rate observation [2]

items.stem: What are the products when aluminium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid?
items.answer: 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂
items.markingKey: 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂

items.stem: A student tests metals P, Q, R with cold water and with dilute hydrochloric acid. P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — reacts steadily with fizzing; Q: cold water — reacts vigorously, fizzing and moving around on the surface; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; R: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles. Deduce the order of reactivity of the metals, most reactive first, and suggest the identity of Q.
items.answer: Q > P > R; Q could be sodium.
items.markingKey: Order Q > P > R [2]; identity consistent with observations [1]

items.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction of sodium with cold water.
items.answer: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂
items.markingKey: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂: formulae [1]; balancing [1]

items.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction of zinc with steam.
items.answer: Zn + H₂O → ZnO + H₂
items.markingKey: Zn + H₂O → ZnO + H₂: formulae [1]; balancing [1]

items.stem: A student tests metals P, Q, R with cold water and with dilute hydrochloric acid. P: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; Q: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; R: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles. Deduce the order of reactivity of the metals, most reactive first, and suggest the identity of P.
items.answer: P > R > Q; P could be magnesium.
items.markingKey: Order P > R > Q [2]; identity consistent with observations [1]

items.stem: A student tests metals P, Q, R, S with cold water and with dilute hydrochloric acid. P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — reacts steadily with fizzing; Q: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; R: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; S: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles. Deduce the order of reactivity of the metals, most reactive first, and suggest the identity of R.
items.answer: R > Q > P > S; R could be potassium.
items.markingKey: Order R > Q > P > S [2]; identity consistent with observations [1]

items.stem: Freya investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; Q: cold water — reacts vigorously, fizzing and moving around on the surface; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; R: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; S: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction. (a) Put the metals in order of reactivity, most reactive first. (b) Predict what would happen if P were added to a solution of copper(II) sulfate. Explain.
items.answer: (a) P > Q > R > S (b) It reacts with the water first: fizzing (hydrogen) and an alkaline hydroxide forms, giving a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide; copper metal is not displaced.

items.stem: Leila investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; Q: cold water — fizzes steadily; the water turns cloudy as calcium hydroxide forms; dilute acid — reacts very vigorously; R: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; S: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing. (a) Which metal(s) are below hydrogen in the reactivity series? Explain. (b) Predict what would happen if R were added to a solution of copper(II) sulfate. Explain.
items.answer: (a) P: they do not react with dilute acid. (b) It reacts with the water first: fizzing (hydrogen) and an alkaline hydroxide forms, giving a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide; copper metal is not displaced.

items.stem: Samuel investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; Q: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; R: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; S: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles. (a) R is magnesium. Write the equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid. (b) Name the gas produced when metals react with dilute acids and give a test for it.
items.answer: (a) Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂ (b) Hydrogen — lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: Which mixture reacts?
items.answer: zinc and copper(II) sulfate solution
items.markingKey: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compounds: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.

items.stem: Explain why copper does not react with zinc sulfate solution.
items.answer: Copper is less reactive than zinc, so it cannot displace zinc from its compound.

items.stem: Explain why the thermite reaction is used to weld railway lines.
items.answer: It is very exothermic; the iron produced is molten and fills the gap between the rails.

items.stem: Predict whether iron reacts with aqueous magnesium sulfate. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction: iron is less reactive than magnesium, so it cannot displace it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A piece of magnesium is placed in aqueous zinc sulfate. Describe what you would see and write the balanced equation and the ionic equation.
items.answer: A grey solid forms on the metal. Mg + ZnSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Zn; ionic: Mg + Zn²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Zn
items.markingKey: 1 mark observation; 1 mark equation; 1 mark ionic equation [3]

items.stem: Elena adds 1.0 g of each metal powder to 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature. Results — copper: start 18.0 °C, highest 18.0 °C; magnesium: start 18.0 °C, highest 60.0 °C; iron: start 18.0 °C, highest 25.0 °C; zinc: start 18.0 °C, highest 30.0 °C. (a) Write the ionic equation for the reaction of magnesium with copper(II) ions. (b) State what is seen in the cup containing magnesium.
items.answer: (a) Mg + Cu²⁺ → Mg²⁺ + Cu (b) Pink-brown solid forms; blue colour fades; the mixture gets hot.

items.stem: What is seen when an iron nail is left in copper(II) sulfate solution?
options: A brown coating forms on the nail and the blue colour fades
Bubbles of hydrogen form and the solution turns blue
The nail dissolves completely and the solution turns colourless
items.answer: A brown coating forms on the nail and the blue colour fades
items.markingKey: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu: copper deposits; solution becomes pale green.

items.stem: Explain why the displacement of copper by magnesium is a redox reaction.
items.answer: Magnesium atoms lose electrons (oxidised) to form Mg²⁺; copper(II) ions gain electrons (reduced) to form copper atoms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why the temperature rise is larger when magnesium, rather than iron, is added to copper(II) sulfate solution.
items.answer: Magnesium is further above copper in the reactivity series, so the reaction releases more energy.

items.stem: Explain why the sulfate ions are described as spectator ions in Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
items.answer: They are present in solution before and after the reaction and are not changed.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the sulfate ions are described as spectator ions in Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. (b) Explain why the thermite reaction is used to weld railway lines.
items.answer: (a) They are present in solution before and after the reaction and are not changed. (b) It is very exothermic; the iron produced is molten and fills the gap between the rails.

items.stem: 1.12 g of iron powder is added to excess silver nitrate solution. Fe + 2AgNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. Calculate the mass of silver that is displaced.
4.00 g of copper(II) oxide is heated with excess magnesium powder. Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu. Calculate the mass of copper produced.
16.0 g of zinc oxide is heated with excess magnesium powder. Mg + ZnO → MgO + Zn. Calculate the mass of zinc produced and identify the oxidising agent.
items.answer: 12.8 g; zinc oxide is the oxidising agent
items.markingKey: n(ZnO) = 16.0/81 = 0.198 mol [1]; n(Zn) = 0.198 mol [1]; mass = 12.8 g [1]; oxidising agent [1]

items.stem: Tariq places a strip of iron into aqueous silver nitrate. Fe + 2AgNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. (a) Write the ionic equation. (b) Write the half-equation for the change to the iron atoms. (c) Name the spectator ion.
items.answer: (a) Fe + 2Ag⁺ → Fe²⁺ + 2Ag (b) Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (c) nitrate ion

items.stem: Yusuf adds 1.0 g of each metal powder to 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ copper(II) sulfate solution in a polystyrene cup and records the temperature. Results — iron: start 20.0 °C, highest 27.0 °C; magnesium: start 20.0 °C, highest 61.0 °C; silver: start 20.0 °C, highest 20.0 °C; zinc: start 20.0 °C, highest 32.0 °C. (a) Calculate the temperature rise for each metal. (b) State two variables that must be controlled. (c) Explain why silver gives no temperature rise.
items.answer: (a) iron 7 °C; magnesium 41 °C; silver 0 °C; zinc 12 °C (b) Mass/particle size of metal; volume, concentration and starting temperature of copper(II) sulfate. (c) Silver is less reactive than copper, so no displacement occurs.

items.stem: The reactivity of a metal depends on
options: how easily its atoms lose electrons to form positive ions
how easily its atoms gain electrons
the size of its nucleus only
items.answer: how easily its atoms lose electrons to form positive ions
items.markingKey: More reactive metals form positive ions more readily.

items.stem: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium in terms of electron loss.
items.answer: Potassium’s outer electron is further from the nucleus (more shells, more shielding), so it is lost more easily to form K⁺.

items.stem: Explain how the oxide layer on aluminium can be made thicker, and why this is useful.
items.answer: By anodising (electrolysis with aluminium as the anode); the thicker oxide layer gives even better protection against corrosion and can be dyed.

items.stem: Write the half-equation for calcium atoms forming calcium ions, and state whether this is oxidation or reduction.
items.answer: Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻; oxidation (loss of electrons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark half-equation; 1 mark oxidation with reason [2]

items.stem: Put zinc, sodium, copper in order of their tendency to form positive ions, greatest first, and write the half-equation for the ion formation of the most reactive one.
items.answer: sodium > zinc > copper; Na → Na⁺ + e⁻
items.markingKey: 1 mark order (same as reactivity series); 1 mark half-equation [2]

items.stem: A drinks company uses aluminium cans, even though aluminium is more reactive than iron. (a) Explain why the foil in acid reacts only after a delay. (b) Suggest why aluminium is placed above zinc in the reactivity series even though it often reacts more slowly.
items.answer: (a) The acid must first react with/remove the oxide layer; then the metal is exposed and reacts. (b) Once the oxide layer is removed, aluminium loses electrons more readily than zinc; its position reflects its tendency to form positive ions.

items.stem: Why does aluminium appear less reactive than its position in the reactivity series suggests?
options: It is coated with a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide
It has a very high density
items.answer: It is coated with a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide
items.markingKey: The Al₂O₃ layer stops water and acids reaching the metal.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a displacement reaction, the more reactive metal (b) Define oxidation in terms of electrons.
items.answer: (a) is oxidised (b) Oxidation is the loss of electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) It loses electrons to form positive ions. (b) [1]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of electrons, why magnesium displaces copper from copper(II) sulfate solution.
items.answer: Magnesium has a greater tendency to lose electrons; Mg atoms give electrons to Cu²⁺ ions, forming Mg²⁺ and Cu atoms.

items.stem: Explain why aluminium powder reacts quickly with acid while aluminium foil reacts slowly at first.
items.answer: Powder has a larger surface area, and the oxide layer on foil must first be removed before the metal reacts.

items.stem: Explain why gold is found uncombined in the Earth’s crust.
items.answer: Gold has very little tendency to form positive ions, so it does not react with oxygen, water or acids.

items.stem: Put calcium, magnesium, aluminium in order of their tendency to form positive ions, greatest first, and write the half-equation for the ion formation of the most reactive one.
items.answer: calcium > magnesium > aluminium; Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: 1 mark order (same as reactivity series); 1 mark half-equation [2]

items.stem: Write the half-equation for potassium atoms forming potassium ions, and state whether this is oxidation or reduction.
items.answer: K → K⁺ + e⁻; oxidation (loss of electrons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark half-equation; 1 mark oxidation with reason [2]

items.stem: In a water-testing laboratory, a piece of aluminium foil is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. For several minutes nothing happens, then the foil starts to fizz steadily. (a) Write the balanced equation for aluminium reacting with hydrochloric acid. (b) State whether aluminium is oxidised or reduced when it forms ions, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) 2Al + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂ (b) Oxidised: it loses electrons.

items.stem: Jonas places a strip of copper into aqueous silver nitrate. Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. (a) Describe what would be seen. (b) Write the ionic equation.
items.answer: (a) Shiny grey/silver crystals form on the metal. (b) Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag

items.stem: In a chemistry club, a piece of aluminium foil is placed in dilute hydrochloric acid. For several minutes nothing happens, then the foil starts to fizz steadily. items.stem: The position of hydrogen in the reactivity series shows that

metals below it react with water
items.answer: metals above it can displace hydrogen from dilute acids
items.markingKey: Metals more reactive than hydrogen react with dilute acids to give H₂.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Describe how you could use dilute hydrochloric acid to put zinc, iron and magnesium into a reactivity order. (b) Explain why potassium and dilute hydrochloric acid are never reacted in a school laboratory.
items.answer: (a) Add equal-sized pieces to equal volumes of the same acid at the same temperature; compare the rate of bubbling (or gas volume in a set time); faster = more reactive. (b) Potassium is so reactive that the reaction would be explosive.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark fair test; 1 mark rate observation [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction of potassium with cold water.
items.answer: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂
items.markingKey: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂: formulae [1]; balancing [1]

items.stem: A student tests metals P, Q, R with cold water and with dilute hydrochloric acid. P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; Q: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing; R: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test. Deduce the order of reactivity of the metals, most reactive first, and suggest the identity of R.
items.answer: R > Q > P; R could be potassium.
items.markingKey: Order R > Q > P [2]; identity consistent with observations [1]

items.stem: Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction of magnesium with steam.
items.answer: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂
items.markingKey: Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂: formulae [1]; balancing [1]

items.stem: Zara investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — fizzes steadily; the water turns cloudy as calcium hydroxide forms; dilute acid — reacts very vigorously; Q: cold water — reacts vigorously, fizzing and moving around on the surface; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; R: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — no reaction; S: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles. (a) P is calcium. Write the equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid. (b) Predict what would happen if Q were added to a solution of copper(II) sulfate. Explain.
items.answer: (a) Ca + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂ (b) It reacts with the water first: fizzing (hydrogen) and an alkaline hydroxide forms, giving a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide; copper metal is not displaced.

items.stem: Omar investigates four metals, labelled P, Q, R, S. Results — P: cold water — no reaction; dilute acid — reacts steadily with fizzing; Q: cold water — no reaction (rusts very slowly); dilute acid — reacts slowly with a few bubbles; R: cold water — reacts very vigorously; the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; dilute acid — too dangerous to test; S: cold water — reacts very slowly; a few bubbles over several days; dilute acid — reacts vigorously with rapid fizzing. (a) Which metal(s) are below hydrogen in the reactivity series? Explain. (b) P is zinc. Write the equation for its reaction with hydrochloric acid.
items.answer: (a) None: every metal reacts with dilute acid (or water), so all are above hydrogen. (b) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂

items.stem: In the reaction Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu, which substance is reduced?
items.answer: copper(II) oxide
items.markingKey: CuO loses oxygen (Cu²⁺ gains electrons) — it is reduced; Mg is oxidised.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the temperature rise is larger when magnesium, rather than iron, is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. (b) Explain why the sulfate ions are described as spectator ions in Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
items.answer: (a) Magnesium is further above copper in the reactivity series, so the reaction releases more energy. (b) They are present in solution before and after the reaction and are not changed.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the temperature rise is larger when magnesium, rather than iron, is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. (b) Explain why the thermite reaction is used to weld railway lines.
items.answer: (a) Magnesium is further above copper in the reactivity series, so the reaction releases more energy. (b) It is very exothermic; the iron produced is molten and fills the gap between the rails.

items.stem: Predict whether silver reacts with aqueous iron(II) sulfate. Explain your answer.
items.answer: No reaction: silver is less reactive than iron, so it cannot displace it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark prediction; 1 mark reason [2]

items.stem: A piece of lead is placed in aqueous silver nitrate. Describe what you would see and write the balanced equation and the ionic equation.
items.answer: Shiny grey/silver crystals form on the metal. Pb + 2AgNO₃ → Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag; ionic: Pb + 2Ag⁺ → Pb²⁺ + 2Ag
items.markingKey: 1 mark observation; 1 mark equation; 1 mark ionic equation [3]

items.stem: Omar places a strip of magnesium into aqueous silver nitrate. Mg + 2AgNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. (a) Write the ionic equation. (b) Explain why the reaction would not occur if silver were placed in a solution of magnesium ions. (c) Name the spectator ion.
items.answer: (a) Mg + 2Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2Ag (b) Silver is less reactive; it has less tendency to form positive ions than magnesium. (c) nitrate ion

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Define reduction in terms of electrons. (b) Why does aluminium appear less reactive than its position in the reactivity series suggests?
items.answer: (a) Reduction is the gain of electrons. (b) It is coated with a thin, unreactive layer of aluminium oxide
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) The Al₂O₃ layer stops water and acids reaching the metal.

items.stem: Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag. Use ideas about electron transfer to explain which species is oxidised and which is reduced, and why this shows copper is more reactive than silver.
items.answer: Copper atoms lose electrons (oxidised) to form ions; silver ions gain electrons (reduced) to form atoms. Copper has the greater tendency to form positive ions, so it is more reactive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark oxidised species; 1 mark reduced species; 1 mark link to tendency to form positive ions [3]

items.stem: Mg + 2Ag⁺ → Mg²⁺ + 2Ag. Use ideas about electron transfer to explain which species is oxidised and which is reduced, and why this shows magnesium is more reactive than silver.
items.answer: Magnesium atoms lose electrons (oxidised) to form ions; silver ions gain electrons (reduced) to form atoms. Magnesium has the greater tendency to form positive ions, so it is more reactive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark oxidised species; 1 mark reduced species; 1 mark link to tendency to form positive ions [3]

items.stem: Write the half-equation for silver atoms forming silver ions, and state whether this is oxidation or reduction.
items.answer: Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻; oxidation (loss of electrons).
items.markingKey: 1 mark half-equation; 1 mark oxidation with reason [2]

items.stem: Ravi notices that aluminium window frames in Cairo have lasted for decades without corroding, even though aluminium is high in the reactivity series. Write the equation for the formation of the oxide layer.
items.answer: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃

items.stem: Freya places a strip of iron into aqueous copper(II) sulfate. Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu. (a) Write the ionic equation. (b) Write the half-equation for the change to the iron atoms. (c) Explain, in terms of electrons, which substance is the reducing agent. (d) Name the spectator ion.
items.answer: (a) Fe + Cu²⁺ → Fe²⁺ + Cu (b) Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (c) Iron: it gives (loses) electrons to the copper ions. (d) sulfate ion
